Start with the grade columns that appear in at least one feasible card. If every such column in one domain can
be combined with every such column in the other, the feasible cards form a Cartesian product. With additive
expected loss, choosing a column with the lowest weighted loss in each domain then gives a joint optimum.
Every combination of tied minima is also optimal.
This condition can hold even when outcomes are dependent. A joint cap can rule out some combinations
even when outcomes are independent.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Dependent domains, separate choices.** Coincident reversals give a feasible product of all nine cards.
  Both domains prefer A ahead, with total risk 1/10, even though their targets are dependent.
- **Different dependence, same minimum.** Disjoint reversals leave each domain's distribution and weighted
  losses unchanged. With the joint cap disabled, stating A ahead in both domains still gives the unique
  optimum at risk 1/10.
- **Zero loss weight in S.** All three S columns have the same weighted loss, and C still favors A ahead.
  The three resulting cards tie at risk 1/10. Their unweighted losses in S differ.
- **Independent domains with a joint guard.** The feasible family has three cards and fails the product condition.
  The two domain minima sum to 1/10, but the card that combines them has joint-event probability 19/100,
  above the cap 3/20. The two feasible optima each state a direction in one domain, at risk 7/40.
- **Joint guard with coincident failures.** Four feasible cards form a product of two columns per domain.
  The best card states A ahead in both domains. Its risk and joint-event probability are both 1/10.

With independent reversals, zero S weight, and an active cap, a feasible card still reaches the lower bound
of 1/10. Some combinations of weighted minima exceed the cap, but only one needs to pass to reach the bound.
Errors in S still count toward the cap when its loss weight is zero.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The fictional distributions have the same marginals. The calculation evaluates the nine cards in this
example, with expected-error caps disabled and the joint cap set separately. A shared grade leaves the
direction unstated. If the supplied law approximates another posterior, feasibility under that posterior
requires a separate check.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
The [R script](../../data/recipes/profile-separability.R) reproduces all twelve settings with postrank 1.2.0
and gmp. It uses the public results to identify each domain's feasible columns and weighted minima.

```r
source("profile-separability.R")
result <- profile_separability()
result$summary
```
:::

Source: [postrank multidomain decisions](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank/articles/mdomain-decisions.html).
